text: Smallholder farmers in Preah Vihear may earn livestock income from milk, eggs, chicks, and breeding animals as well as live-animal sales, but the importance of each depends on the farming system. Village chicken production is widespread — Cambodian poultry-market research found over 80% of smallholders kept local breeds, which also accounted for most chickens and ducks sold in surveyed markets. Dairy cattle are different: Cambodia has crossbred dairy cattle and milk-producing farms, but dairy is not assumed to be a normal or established income activity for every Preah Vihear smallholder without farmer-specific confirmation. Where milk is sold, hygiene, rapid delivery, and temperature control are critical because raw milk is highly perishable — "keep milk clean, keep it as cool as practical, and deliver it promptly" is more realistic than assuming refrigeration is available. Eggs are often a more realistic recurring smallholder product; farmers should collect regularly and protect eggs from sunlight, heat, rain, breakage, and manure contamination. During the wet season (roughly May–October), rain and muddy roads complicate transport and hygiene for milk and eggs; during the dry season (roughly November–April, with temperatures commonly exceeding 32°C before the rains), heat accelerates spoilage of both. A productive animal (laying hen, dairy cow) has ongoing earning value — compare one-time sale revenue against repeated product income minus feed/health/mortality costs before selling a productive animal. No specific poultry or dairy-cattle breed is assumed characteristic of Preah Vihear without local evidence. Milk is not assumed to be pasteurized or automatically safe just because it is fresh — brucellosis can transmit through infected milk, and applicable Cambodian food-safety requirements should be checked before informal raw-milk sale.
